answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — adapted from Kenneth B. Elliott
answer.authorDates: American sales executive · Vice-President in Charge of Sales, The Studebaker Corporation, 1940s
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Gandhi wrote or said this. The wording descends from a customer-relations creed articulated by Kenneth B. Elliott of Studebaker in ‘Printers’ Ink’ (May 1941) — “The customer is not an interruption of our work — he is the purpose of it.” The “patient / hospital” version is a later, anonymous healthcare rewording; Gandhi’s name was attached only from the 1970s, decades after his death in 1948.

source.excerpt: A patient is the most important person in our hospital. He is not an interruption to our work, he is the purpose of it.
trail: The definitive investigation is Quote Investigator’s trace of the “customer” creed to Kenneth B. Elliott in ‘Printers’ Ink’, May 1941 ↗, with Gandhi attributions surfacing only in the 1970s.

The full creed — “A customer is the most important visitor on our premises… he is not an interruption in our work, he is the purpose of it” — is catalogued under Kenneth B. Elliott (and tagged “misattributed-to-gandhi”) ↗.
Fact-checkers list the customer version among fabricated Gandhi lines: “probably from a VP at the Studebaker car company circa 1941” ↗.
source.excerptNote: The healthcare rewording. Elliott’s 1941 original spoke of “the customer” and “our premises,” not patients or hospitals.

source.rightsNote: The exact “patient / hospital” wording is an anonymous later adaptation with no identifiable published source, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. Its ancestor — Kenneth B. Elliott’s customer creed — was first published in ‘Printers’ Ink’ in May 1941 and would itself be a 1941 U.S. periodical publication, not a Gandhi work.

author.metaLine: American sales executive · Vice-President in Charge of Sales, The Studebaker Corporation (1940s)
author.bio: Kenneth B. Elliott was a Studebaker sales executive whose set of customer-relations principles appeared in a May 1941 interview in the advertising trade journal ‘Printers’ Ink’. His second principle — “the customer is not an interruption of our work — he is the purpose of it” — is the earliest documented form of the line now widely and wrongly stamped with Gandhi’s name. The “patient” and “hospital” wording is a later, anonymous adaptation of Elliott’s business creed.

misattribution.heading: A business creed dressed up as Gandhi
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable fake Gandhi quotes — a mid-century sales-and-service maxim recast for hospitals and pinned on a moral icon who died before it was ever linked to him.

items.why: No speech, book, letter, or article by Gandhi contains this line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds Gandhi attributions only from the 1970s — more than two decades after his 1948 death — and calls them unconvincing.
The wording first appears as a customer-relations creed in ‘Printers’ Ink’, May 1941 ↗, though even Elliott may have been repeating existing trade wisdom.

items.who: L.L. Bean, Paul T. Babson, Ray Noyes
items.why: Through the 1940s–50s the same principles were variously attributed to a cluster of businessmen — a classic sign of a floating maxim with no single fixed author, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the line is a 1941 customer-service creed — earliest tied to Studebaker’s Kenneth B. Elliott — reworded for hospitals and misattributed to Gandhi decades after his death, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Gandhi
lead: The sentiment — that the person you serve is the purpose of your work, not a distraction from it — is genuinely appealing, which is exactly why it drifts toward revered names. A sales maxim about car buyers gains gravity when it seems to come from a moral teacher, and hospitals in particular found the “patient” rewording irresistible for mission statements and waiting-room posters.

The attribution fails on the timeline alone: the wording is documented in 1941, Gandhi died in 1948, and his name only attaches to it in the 1970s. Feel-good lines with no citation are precisely the kind that accrete to Gandhi — he is one of the internet’s single biggest magnets for fabricated quotes.
context.pull: A 1941 sales creed, reworded for hospitals and signed with Gandhi’s name.
